mainTopic: Who goes to גלות: the downward-motion rule, the slipping ladder rung, the butcher, and the ax that slips
overview: The משנה ends with a rule: an accidental killer goes to גלות only if the killing came through a downward motion. שמואל finds the source in the פסוק 'וַיַּפֵּל עָלָיו'. A ברייתא then reads the פסוקים word by word. רבא and רבה explain that its 'מזיד' and 'מתכוין' mean an אומר מותר and someone who aimed at a different target. Another ברייתא lists cases left out of גלות (a corner, an enemy, a wrong throw) and cases brought in (a shove, or a downward motion done in order to go up). רבי יוחנן uses that last idea to rule that a climber whose ladder rung slips and kills goes to גלות. He defends this by showing that the משנה's זה הכלל comes to add a butcher, whose four ברייתות all follow the direction of the swing. The גמרא then rejects the idea that two ladder ברייתות argue about up or down, and settles them in three other ways. A new משנה brings a מחלוקת between רבי and חכמים about an ax head slipping off its handle versus a chip flying off the wood. רב explains that they argue whether we learn from the spelling (יש אם למסורת) or the reading (יש אם למקרא). The גמרא begins to question whether רבי really holds יש אם למסורת, and this continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Climbing up a ladder and falling: no exile
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that someone climbing up a ladder who falls on a person and kills him does not go to גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was climbing up a ladder, fell on someone and killed him, he is not exiled.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a case where an accidental killer does not go to גלות, because he was moving upward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the משנה said that someone coming down a ladder who falls and kills is exiled. Here the motion is upward, so the result is the opposite. Both cases are accidental killing; the difference is only the direction of the motion.

keyTerms.meaning: Goes into exile to a city of refuge

phrases.english: If he was climbing up a ladder
and he fell on him and killed him
this one is not exiled.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: An accidental killing that happens while moving upward does not bring גלות.

steps.title: The general rule: downward motion means exile
steps.stepSummary: The משנה sums up its cases: a killing through a downward motion brings גלות, and one not through a downward motion does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: whoever killed through his downward motion is exiled, and whoever did not kill through his downward motion is not exiled.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה wraps up all its examples with one general principle about the direction of motion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of listing every case, the משנה gives a test that works for all of them. The question is whether the killing happened while something was moving down. Only then does גלות apply.

keyTerms.meaning: In the course of his downward motion

steps.whatToRemember: For גלות, the killing has to happen through a downward motion. Upward motion means no גלות.

phrases.english: This is the general rule:
anyone who killed through his downward motion is exiled,
and one who did not kill through his downward motion is not exiled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the ladder cases into one general principle.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: גלות applies only to an accidental killing done through a downward motion.

steps.title: Where does the downward rule come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the משנה's downward-motion rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by asking for the source of the משנה's rule. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה stated the rule without a source. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches that only a downward motion brings גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that follows the משנה
From where do we know these things? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: Gemara:
From where do we know these things?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the rule that only a downward motion brings גלות.

steps.title: שמואל's source: 'and he caused it to fall'
steps.stepSummary: שמואל derives the rule from the פסוק 'וַיַּפֵּל עָלָיו וַיָּמֹת': there is גלות only when the killing happens through falling.
steps.simpleTranslation: As שמואל said: the פסוק says 'and he caused it to fall upon him and he died', which means there is no גלות unless it falls in a downward way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with a פסוק quoted by שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'וַיַּפֵּל' means 'caused to fall', which is a downward motion. From this word, שמואל learns that גלות applies only when the deadly motion is a fall, a downward movement.

keyTerms.meaning: And he caused it to fall

phrases.english: As Shmuel said,
for the verse says:
"and he caused it to fall upon him and he died"
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:23

phrases.english: meaning: not unless it falls in a downward way.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'וַיַּפֵּל' in במדבר 35:23 teaches that גלות applies only to a killing through a downward fall.
steps.whatToRemember: The source for the downward rule is 'וַיַּפֵּל עָלָיו וַיָּמֹת', as שמואל explains.

steps.title: ברייתא: two words that exclude intentional killers
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from 'בִּשְׁגָגָה' that a מזיד is excluded from גלות, and from 'בִּבְלִי דַעַת' that a מתכוין is excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'by accident' excludes the intentional killer. 'Without knowing' excludes the one who meant to do it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that uses two words in the Torah to rule out certain killers from גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word in the פסוקים about the accidental killer is read as leaving someone out. 'בִּשְׁגָגָה' leaves out a מזיד, and 'בִּבְלִי דַעַת' leaves out a מתכוין. This sets up the גמרא's question about why the first exclusion is needed at all.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"By accident" excludes the intentional killer.
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:11

phrases.english: "Without knowing" excludes the one who intends.
phrases.notes: דברים 19:4

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוקים exclude a מזיד and a מתכוין from גלות.

steps.title: Why exclude a מזיד? He is executed anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a פסוק is needed to exclude a מזיד from גלות, since a deliberate murderer gets the death penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: An intentional killer? That is obvious. He is liable to the death penalty!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. Excluding a מזיד from גלות seems pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who murders on purpose gets the death penalty, so of course he does not go to גלות. The Torah should not need a word to teach something so obvious. So 'מזיד' must mean something else here.

phrases.english: An intentional killer? That is obvious;
he is liable to the death penalty!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the need for the first exclusion in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A deliberate murderer is executed, so excluding him from גלות needs no פסוק.

steps.title: רבא: 'מזיד' means someone who thought killing was allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the ברייתא's 'מזיד' means an אומר מותר, someone who killed thinking it was permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: say it excludes one who says it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question by changing what 'מזיד' refers to in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אומר מותר is not executed, because he did not knowingly break the law. So it is not obvious that he is left out of גלות, and the פסוק is needed to teach that.

keyTerms.meaning: One who says (thinks) it is permitted

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
Say it excludes one who says it is permitted.
phrases.notes: He means someone who killed thinking that killing this person was allowed.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a term in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מזיד' meant a deliberate murderer, which made the exclusion pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'מזיד' means an אומר מותר, who is not executed, so excluding him from גלות is a real teaching.

steps.title: אביי: Isn't such a person an אנוס?
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that someone who thought killing was permitted is an אנוס, so how can he be called a מזיד?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If he says it is permitted, he is acting under circumstances beyond his control!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person really believed killing was allowed, he did not know any better. That seems like an אנוס, not a מזיד. So calling him 'מזיד' looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: One acting under circumstances beyond his control

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
If he says it is permitted, isn't he acting beyond his control?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי אִי אוֹמֵר מוּתָּר
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reading of 'מזיד' as an אומר מותר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who honestly thought killing was permitted seems to be an אנוס, the opposite of a מזיד.

steps.title: רבא: An אומר מותר is close to a מזיד
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that an אומר מותר is considered close to a מזיד, so the Torah can call him one.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: For I say, one who says it is permitted is close to being intentional.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends his answer against אביי's objection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not treat thinking killing is allowed as an innocent mistake. Such a person should have known better, so he is close to a מזיד. That is why he does not get גלות, even though he is not executed.

keyTerms.meaning: For I say (giving his own reasoning)

steps.whatToRemember: An אומר מותר does not get גלות, because רבא considers him close to a מזיד, not an אנוס.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Close to a מזיד' does not make him a full מזיד. He is not executed like a deliberate murderer, but he is also left out of גלות.

phrases.english: He said to him:
For I say: one who says it is permitted
is close to being intentional.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the category: close to a מזיד, not an אנוס
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An אומר מותר is an אנוס.
steps.terutzMaskana: An אומר מותר is close to a מזיד, so the פסוק excludes him from גלות.

steps.title: Why would we need a פסוק to exclude someone who meant to kill?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the second half of the ברייתא, that בִּבְלִי דַעַת excludes a מתכוין. It asks why this is needed, since someone who kills on purpose gets the death penalty anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said that "unawares" leaves out someone who acted on purpose. But that is obvious, because he deserves death!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the same kind of question it asked on the first half of the ברייתא. This time it asks about the word בִּבְלִי דַעַת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Back in step 6 the גמרא asked why we need a פסוק to exclude a מזיד. Now it asks the same thing about the מתכוין. A person who kills on purpose gets מיתה, so of course he does not go to גלות, and we would not need a פסוק to tell us that.

keyTerms.meaning: "Unawares": without knowing, a phrase from the פסוק about the accidental killer
"It's obvious!": the גמרא's way of saying a teaching seems unnecessary
Someone who deserves the death penalty

phrases.english: "Unawares": to exclude one who acted with intent.
One with intent? It is obvious,
he is subject to death!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the question on the first half of the ברייתא, the גמרא asks the same kind of question on its second half.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's teaching that בִּבְלִי דַעַת excludes a מתכוין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person who kills on purpose already gets מיתה, so a פסוק to exclude him from גלות seems unneeded.

steps.title: רבה: he meant to kill something else and killed a person
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that this מתכוין means someone who meant to kill an animal, a גוי, or a נפל, and killed a person, a Jew, or a viable baby instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: It excludes someone who meant to kill an animal and killed a person, meant to kill a גוי and killed a Jew, or meant to kill a non-viable baby and killed a viable one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the question by explaining which kind of "intent" the ברייתא means. He says the person meant to kill a target for which he would not be punished with death, and he killed a different target instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This person did not mean to kill the one who died, so he does not get מיתה. But he did mean to kill something, so he is not a plain accident either. The פסוק teaches that he does not go to גלות, so the teaching is not obvious after all.

keyTerms.meaning: A baby born unable to survive
A baby born able to live

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this person is as guilty as a regular murderer who gets מיתה. He meant to kill something else, so he is not killed. The פסוק only teaches that he is also not sent to גלות.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
To exclude one who intended to kill the animal
and killed the person,
to kill the gentile and killed a Jew,
to kill the non-viable baby and killed a viable one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10 by changing what the word מתכוין refers to.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the intent was aimed at a different target
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מתכוין means a plain murderer who meant to kill this person, so the teaching would be obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: מתכוין means someone who meant to kill a target he would not get מיתה for, and he hit a person. He is excluded from גלות.

steps.title: A new ברייתא: a corner and an enemy are excluded
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the פסוק about the accidental killer word by word. אִם בְּפֶתַע excludes killing someone at a corner, and בְּלֹא אֵיבָה excludes an enemy.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: "If suddenly" excludes a corner. "Without enmity" excludes an enemy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that explains each word of the פסוק about the accidental killer. This step gives the first two words, and both of them take cases out of גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Suddenly" leaves out someone who ran into another person coming around a corner and killed him. "Without enmity" leaves out a killer who hated the victim. Even if the killing looks like an accident, we assume it was not.

keyTerms.meaning: An enemy, someone who hates the victim

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"If suddenly": to exclude a corner.
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:22. He means someone who bumped into the victim coming around a corner.

phrases.english: "Without enmity": to exclude an enemy.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״אִם בְּפֶתַע״ – פְּרָט לְקֶרֶן זָוִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the first ברייתא to a new ברייתא that reads another פסוק about the accidental killer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Killing at a corner and killing by an enemy are excluded from גלות.

steps.title: A shove and a downward motion for going up are included
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. הֲדָפוֹ includes pushing someone with one's body, and הִשְׁלִיךְ עָלָיו includes a downward motion that is part of an upward one.
steps.simpleTranslation: "He pushed him" means he shoved him with his body. "Or cast upon him" brings in a downward motion that is needed for an upward motion.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now uses two words of the פסוק to add cases that do get גלות. One is shoving with the body. The other is a downward motion done as part of going up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally גלות comes from a downward motion that kills. "Or cast upon him" adds that even a downward motion done in order to go up, like bending down to lift something, still counts as downward for גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: Needed for the purpose of an upward motion

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of יְרִידָה שֶׁהִיא צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה is exactly what רבי יוחנן uses to answer the ladder question at the end of this section.

phrases.english: "He pushed him": that he shoved him with his body.
"Or cast upon him":
to include a downward motion that is for the purpose of an upward motion.
phrases.notes: Picture someone bending down to lift a heavy thing: the bending is downward, but it is part of lifting up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, now with words that add cases to גלות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Shoving with the body, and a downward motion done to go up, both get גלות.

steps.title: Wrong direction and wrong distance are excluded
steps.stepSummary: בְּלֹא צְדִיָּה excludes someone who threw to one side when it went to another side. וַאֲשֶׁר לֹא צָדָה excludes someone who meant to throw two אמות and threw four.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Without lying in wait" excludes someone who aimed to one side and it went to another side. "And who did not lie in wait" excludes someone who meant to throw two אמות and threw four.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings two similar words from two different פסוקים. Each one takes a different throwing mistake out of גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case is a mistake in direction: the stone went to a side he did not aim at. The second is a mistake in distance: it flew farther than he planned. Both are left out of the regular law of גלות.

phrases.english: "Without lying in wait":
to exclude one who intended toward this side
and it went off to a different side.
"And who did not lie in wait":
phrases.notes: שמות 21:13

phrases.aramaic: פְּרָט לְמִתְכַּוֵּין לִזְרוֹק שְׁתַּיִם, וְזָרַק אַרְבַּע.
phrases.english: to exclude one who intended to throw two and threw four.
phrases.notes: Two and four are amounts of distance, measured in אמות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with two words that take throwing mistakes out of גלות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A throw that went in a different direction, or farther than planned, is excluded from גלות.

steps.title: The forest: only a place both people may enter
steps.stepSummary: From "into the forest" the ברייתא learns that גלות applies only where both the victim and the killer were allowed to be.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And one who goes with his friend into the forest": just as both the injured person and the one who caused the harm may enter a forest, so too any place both of them may enter.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by learning a rule about the place where the killing happened. It uses the forest in the פסוק as its model.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A forest is a place anyone may enter. So גלות applies only where both people had permission to be. This leaves out, for example, a victim who entered the killer's property without permission.

keyTerms.meaning: Permission, the right to be there
The one who was harmed, here the victim
The one who caused the harm, here the killer

steps.whatToRemember: This ברייתא reads the פסוקים word by word. Some words take cases out of גלות: a corner, an enemy, the wrong direction, and the wrong distance. Some bring cases in: a shove, and a downward motion done to go up. The forest teaches that גלות applies only where both people were allowed to be.

phrases.english: "And one who comes with his neighbor into the forest":
phrases.notes: דברים 19:5

phrases.english: just as a forest is permitted for the victim and the assailant
to enter there,
so too any place permitted for the victim and the assailant
to enter there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא with a rule about the place of the killing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלות applies only when the killing happened in a place where both victim and killer had permission to be.

steps.title: רבי אבהו asks: a ladder rung slips and kills
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו asks רבי יוחנן about someone climbing a ladder whose rung slipped out, fell, and killed someone. Is that an upward motion or a downward one?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו asked רבי יוחנן: A man was climbing a ladder, a rung slipped out from under him, and it fell and killed someone. What is the law? In a case like this, is it going up or going down?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related question about up and down motions. A man was climbing up, but the rung under his foot went down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His body was going up, but his step pushed the rung downward. If it counts as an upward motion, he would not go to גלות. If it counts as a downward motion, he would.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu asked Rabbi Yoḥanan:
If he was going up a ladder
and a rung slipped out from under him,
and it fell and killed, what is the law?
In a case like this, is it going up,
or is it going down?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the ברייתא's idea of up and down motions with a new, mixed case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a rung that fell while the man was climbing count as an upward motion (no גלות) or a downward motion (גלות)?

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the ברייתא already covered this
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that this case is the ברייתא's יְרִידָה שֶׁהִיא צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה, so it counts as a downward motion and he goes to גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You have already touched on "a downward motion that is for the purpose of an upward motion."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers by pointing back to the ברייתא from step 13. This case fits the rule taught there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pushing the rung down was part of climbing up. That is exactly a downward motion done in order to go up. The ברייתא included that case in גלות, so this man goes to גלות too.

keyTerms.meaning: You touched on, you already reached the case of

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, a rung that slips while someone climbs counts as יְרִידָה שֶׁהִיא צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה, so the climber goes to גלות. This answer is challenged in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: כְּבָר נָגַעְתָּ בִּירִידָה שֶׁהִיא צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה.
phrases.english: You have already touched upon a downward motion that is for the purpose of an upward motion.
phrases.notes: He's pointing back to "or cast upon him" from the ברייתא. That case gets גלות, so this one does too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אבהו's question from step 16 using the ברייתא in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is יְרִידָה שֶׁהִיא צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה, which the ברייתא already included in גלות.

steps.title: The משנה's general rule seems to exempt the ladder case
steps.stepSummary: The rule says that killing 'not in the way of his downward motion' means no גלות. That extra clause seems to be there to cover the ladder climber, who was going up.
steps.simpleTranslation: He challenged him: This is the rule: anyone who kills while moving downward is exiled, and anyone who kills not while moving downward is not exiled. What does 'not while moving downward' come to add? Isn't it a case like this one?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן's ruling about the ladder is challenged from the general rule (זה הכלל) in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A זה הכלל usually comes to add cases the משנה did not spell out. The climber was going up when the rung slipped. So the second clause seems to teach that he is exempt, which goes against רבי יוחנן's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: In the course of his downward motion
He goes into exile (to a city of refuge)
What does it come to add?

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him:
phrases.notes: This is רבי אבהו challenging רבי יוחנן's answer about the ladder.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כׇּל שֶׁבְּדֶרֶךְ יְרִידָתוֹ – גּוֹלֶה,
phrases.english: This is the principle: anyone who kills in the course of his downward motion is exiled,
and one who kills not in the course of his downward motion is not exiled.
"Not in the course of his downward motion": what does it come to add?
Is it not to add a case like this one?
phrases.notes: 'Like this one' means the man going up the ladder whose rung slipped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's answer in Step 17
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the ladder case gets גלות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The extra clause in the general rule must add something, and the ladder case (an upward motion) fits it, which would mean no גלות.

steps.title: The first half of the rule also needs something to add
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן turns the question around: by that logic, what does the first clause 'in the way of his downward motion' come to add?
steps.simpleTranslation: And by your reasoning, what does 'anyone who kills while moving downward' come to add?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן pushes back by asking the same question about the first half of the rule. This sets up his real answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every clause of the rule must add a new case, the first clause needs one too. The ladder case cannot be what both halves add. So there must be some other case that both halves are talking about.

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,
"anyone who kills in the course of his downward motion": what does it come to add?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 18 by turning its own logic back on it
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the second clause must be adding the ladder case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The same reasoning would require the first clause to add something too, so a different case must be meant.

steps.title: Both halves of the rule come to add a butcher
steps.stepSummary: Each half of the rule comes to add the case of a butcher who killed someone while chopping meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the first half comes to add a butcher. Here too, the second half comes to add a butcher.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives his real answer: both clauses of the rule are about a butcher, not the ladder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A butcher's swing has both down parts and up parts. The first clause teaches that a down part gets גלות, and the second teaches that an up part does not. So the second clause is fully used, and the ladder ruling still stands.

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to add a butcher;
here too, it comes to add a butcher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the case that both clauses add, completing the answer begun in Step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the extra clause to a different case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second clause was there to exempt the ladder climber.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both clauses are about a butcher's swing, so they say nothing against רבי יוחנן's ladder ruling.

steps.title: Four ברייתות about a butcher seem to contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: Four ברייתות about a butcher who killed while chopping give four different rulings about a victim in front of him or behind him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: a butcher who was chopping. One ברייתא says: in front of him he is liable, behind him he is exempt. Another says: behind him he is liable, in front of him he is exempt. Another says: both in front and behind he is liable. Another says: both in front and behind he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the butcher ברייתות that the rule is pointing to. On the surface, they all disagree with each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every possible combination appears: front only, back only, both, and neither. This looks like a full contradiction. It sets up the next step, where the גמרא will show they all fit together.

phrases.english: As it is taught: a butcher who was chopping,

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא חֲדָא: לְפָנָיו – חַיָּיב, לְאַחֲרָיו – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: one ברייתא teaches: if he killed someone in front of him, he is liable; behind him, he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ: לְאַחֲרָיו – חַיָּיב, לְפָנָיו – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: And another ברייתא teaches: behind him, he is liable; in front of him, he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ: בֵּין לְפָנָיו בֵּין לְאַחֲרָיו – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: And another ברייתא teaches: whether in front of him or behind him, he is liable.

phrases.aramaic: וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ: בֵּין לְפָנָיו בֵּין לְאַחֲרָיו – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: And another ברייתא teaches: whether in front of him or behind him, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the butcher case mentioned in Step 20
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Four ברייתות give opposite rulings for a butcher who kills in front of or behind himself.

steps.title: The first two ברייתות: down in front and up behind, or the reverse
steps.stepSummary: The first two ברייתות do not argue. One is about a swing going down in front and up behind, and the other is about a swing going up in front and down behind.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is not difficult. Here, it is a downward motion in front and an upward motion behind. There, it is an upward motion in front and a downward motion behind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins solving the contradiction by matching the first two ברייתות to different stages of the butcher's swing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A butcher swings the cleaver back and up, then forward and down, so each side gets both up and down movements. The person hit during the downward part is the one who causes liability. So 'front' or 'behind' is not the real issue.

keyTerms.meaning: Here... there (this source is about one case, that source about another)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think 'in front of him' always means liable. The deciding question is whether the cleaver was moving down or up at that moment.

phrases.english: And it is not difficult.
Here, it is a downward motion in front of him and an upward motion behind him.
phrases.notes: This explains the first ברייתא: liable in front, exempt behind.

phrases.english: There, it is an upward motion in front of him and a downward motion behind him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the first two ברייתות from Step 21
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources into different cases (כאן... כאן)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתות disagree about front versus behind.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each ברייתא is about a different direction of motion. Liability follows the downward motion.

steps.title: The last two ברייתות: down on both sides, or up on both sides
steps.stepSummary: The 'liable both ways' ברייתא is about a downward motion in front and behind. The 'exempt both ways' ברייתא is about an upward motion in front and behind.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, it is a downward motion both in front of him and behind him. There, it is an upward motion both in front of him and behind him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes solving the contradiction by explaining the last two ברייתות the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now all four ברייתות agree: downward means liable and upward means exempt, wherever the victim stood. These are the two clauses of the זה הכלל, so the second clause is used up by the butcher. That answers the challenge, and רבי יוחנן's ladder ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Both the one in front of him and the one behind him

steps.whatToRemember: For גלות, the deciding factor is the direction of the motion. Down means he goes to גלות, and up means he does not, whether the victim was in front or behind. Both halves of the משנה's זה הכלל add the butcher, so they do not exempt the ladder case.
steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps רבי יוחנן's ruling that a slipping ladder rung counts as a downward motion. It also shows that the extra clauses of a זה הכלל can be fully explained without that case.

phrases.english: Here, it is a downward motion both in front of him and behind him;
there, it is an upward motion both in front of him and behind him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the resolution started in Step 22
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources into different cases (כאן... כאן)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'liable both ways' and 'exempt both ways' ברייתות disagree.
steps.terutzMaskana: One is about downward motion on both sides, the other about upward motion on both sides. Liability always follows the downward motion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Liability for גלות follows the downward motion. The זה הכלל adds the butcher, so the challenge to רבי יוחנן is answered.

steps.title: Suggesting the ladder question is a dispute of two ברייתות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that two contradicting ברייתות about a climber whose rung slipped argue over whether this counts as a downward or upward motion.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is like a dispute of תנאים. If someone was climbing a ladder and a rung slipped out from under him, one ברייתא teaches he is liable and another teaches he is exempt. Isn't it that they argue about this: one Sage holds it counts as a downward motion, and the other holds it counts as an upward motion?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to show that the ladder question was already argued about by תנאים, in two ברייתות that give opposite rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we learned that a killing during a downward motion leads to גלות, but one during an upward motion does not. Here one ברייתא says 'liable' and one says 'exempt' about the ladder case. The גמרא suggests the reason is that they disagree about which kind of motion this is.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it is like a dispute of תנאים, a suggestion that an open question was already argued about in older sources
Downward motion, which leads to גלות
Upward motion, which is exempt from גלות
Is it not that...? The גמרא proposing its reading of a source

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of תנאים:
If someone was climbing up a ladder
and a rung slipped out from under him,
one ברייתא teaches he is liable,
and another ברייתא teaches he is exempt.
Is it not that they argue about this:
one Sage holds it is a downward motion,
and the other Sage holds it is an upward motion?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the butcher ברייתות and returns to רבי אבהו's ladder question from step 16, which רבי יוחנן answered in step 17. It suggests that the same question was already argued about by תנאים.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אבהו's question of whether a slipping rung on the way up counts as a downward or upward motion.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Two ברייתות that give opposite rulings, liable and exempt, about the climber whose rung slipped.

steps.title: Everyone agrees it is upward: one ברייתא is about damages and one is about גלות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. All agree it is an upward motion. The 'liable' ברייתא is about paying damages, and the 'exempt' ברייתא is about גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees it is an upward motion. And it is not difficult: here the ברייתא is talking about damages, and there it is talking about גלות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back. The two ברייתות are not arguing about the motion at all. They are talking about two different kinds of liability.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since all agree it is an upward motion, the climber is exempt from גלות, and that is the 'exempt' ברייתא. The 'liable' ברייתא is about paying for damage, where upward or downward makes no difference. So the contradiction disappears without any dispute between תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: Damages, money owed for harm caused
Exile to a city of refuge for an accidental killer
Here... there: splitting two sources into two different cases

steps.confusionAlert: Being exempt from גלות does not mean he is free of all responsibility. He can still be liable to pay damages.

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees it is an upward motion.
And it is not difficult:
here it is about damages,
there it is about exile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggested dispute of תנאים from step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתות argue about downward versus upward motion.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתות can be about different kinds of liability, so there is no need to make them argue.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources into different legal areas: damages versus גלות
steps.terutzMaskana: It is an upward motion according to all. He is liable for damages but exempt from גלות.

steps.title: Second answer: both are about גלות, and it depends on whether the rung was worm-eaten
steps.stepSummary: Another way: both ברייתות are about גלות. He is liable if the rung was worm-eaten and exempt if it was not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say both ברייתות are about גלות, and it is not difficult. This one is where the rung was worm-eaten, and that one is where it was not worm-eaten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to settle the contradiction while keeping both ברייתות about גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rung was worm-eaten, the climber should have been careful before stepping on it, so he is liable to גלות. If it was healthy, he could not have known it would slip, so he is exempt. The difference is how careless he was, not which direction he was moving.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: introduces another possible answer
This one and that one, meaning both sources
Was worm-eaten or rotted by worms

phrases.english: If you want, say both this one and that one are about exile,
and it is not difficult:
this one is where the rung was worm-eaten,
phrases.notes: This is the 'liable' ברייתא. He should have noticed the weak rung.

phrases.english: that one is where it was not worm-eaten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer instead of the damages-versus-גלות split.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the condition of the rung
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seem to argue about the same case of גלות.
steps.terutzMaskana: A worm-eaten rung means he was careless and goes to גלות. A healthy rung was beyond his control, so he is exempt.

steps.title: Third answer: it depends on whether the rung was tightly fitted
steps.stepSummary: Another way: both cases have a healthy rung. He is exempt if it was tightly fitted and liable if it was loose.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say both are where the rung was not worm-eaten, and it is not difficult. This one is where it was tightly fitted, and that one is where it was not tightly fitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer that works even when the rung was healthy in both cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tightly fitted rung gave him no reason to expect it to slip, so he is exempt. A loose rung should have warned him, so he is liable to גלות. Like the second answer, this one turns on whether he could have known about the danger.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא does not accept that the ladder ברייתות argue about upward versus downward. The first answer says all agree it is upward, so one ברייתא is about damages and the other about גלות. The other two answers keep both ברייתות about גלות and split them by whether he could have foreseen the danger: worm-eaten versus healthy, or loose versus tight.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּלָא אַתְלַע,
phrases.english: And if you want, say both this one and that one are where the rung was not worm-eaten,
and it is not difficult:
this one is where it was tightly fitted,
phrases.notes: This is the 'exempt' ברייתא. He had no reason to suspect the rung.

phrases.english: and that one is where it was not tightly fitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּלָא אַתְלַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a third answer. It keeps the healthy-rung case from step 26 and splits it further.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by how firmly the rung was fitted
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If both rungs were healthy, the two ברייתות would seem to truly argue.
steps.terutzMaskana: A tightly fitted rung means he is exempt. A loose rung means he is liable to גלות.

steps.title: Blade slips off the handle versus chip flies off the wood
steps.stepSummary: The משנה records a מחלוקת between רבי and חכמים in two cases: the iron slipping off its handle, and a piece flying off the wood being split.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the iron head slips off its handle and kills someone, רבי says he does not go to גלות, and חכמים say he does. If a piece of the wood being chopped flies off and kills, רבי says he goes to גלות, and חכמים say he does not.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens with two cases of accidental killing while chopping wood, and רבי and חכמים argue about both of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two opinions are mirror images. רבי sends to גלות only when the killing piece came from the tree being chopped. חכמים send to גלות only when the iron came off its own handle.

keyTerms.meaning: the iron, meaning the ax head
goes into exile to an עיר מקלט
the wood that is being split

steps.whatToRemember: Iron off the handle: רבי says no גלות, חכמים say גלות. Chip off the chopped wood: רבי says גלות, חכמים say no גלות.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the sides. Each opinion flips between the two cases, so in each case רבי and חכמים say the opposite of each other.

phrases.english: MISHNA
If the iron slipped off its handle and killed,
Rabbi says: he is not exiled,
and the Rabbis say: he is exiled.
If it came from the wood being split,
phrases.notes: He means a chip of the log he was chopping flew off and killed someone.

phrases.english: Rabbi says: he is exiled,
and the Rabbis say: he is not exiled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of the ladder rung.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי: iron off the handle means no גלות, a chip from the chopped wood means גלות. חכמים: the reverse.

steps.title: רבי proves from the verse that the killing piece comes from the tree
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records רבי's two proofs: the פסוק says 'from the wood' and not 'from its wood', and the word עץ earlier in the same פסוק means the tree being chopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said to חכמים: Does the פסוק say 'the iron slips from its own wood'? It only says 'from the wood'! Also, the word 'wood' appears twice in the פסוק. The first time it means the tree being chopped, so the second time also means the tree being chopped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי proves his view from the wording of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First proof: if the Torah meant the handle, it would say 'its wood'. Saying 'the wood' points to the tree. Second proof: the same word עץ appears earlier in the פסוק about cutting the tree, so the later עץ should mean the same tree.

keyTerms.meaning: from its own wood, meaning the handle
below / above, meaning later and earlier in the same פסוק

phrases.english: GEMARA
It is taught: Rabbi said to the Rabbis:
Is it said, "and the iron slips from its wood"?
phrases.notes: דברים 19:5. רבי is pointing out that the פסוק does not actually say these words.

phrases.english: But it only says "from the wood"!
And furthermore, "wood" is said below,
and "wood" is said above;
phrases.notes: Earlier in the same פסוק: he swings the ax 'to cut the wood.'

phrases.english: just as "wood" said above
is the wood being split,
so too "wood" said below
is the wood being split.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר לָהֶם רַבִּי לַחֲכָמִים: וְכִי נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבי's view in the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רבי's view that גלות applies when the killing piece came from the tree being chopped
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 19:5: the wording 'מן העץ' and the matching use of עץ earlier in the פסוק

steps.title: Both sides read the same word, written one way and read another
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the מחלוקת depends on the word ונשל. רבי follows the written letters (ונישל, 'it made something slip off'). חכמים follow the reading aloud (ונשל, 'it slipped off').
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אשי said in the name of רב: Both sides learned from one פסוק, 'and the iron slips from the wood.' רבי holds that the written spelling is what counts, and it can be read ונישל, meaning the iron knocked off a piece of the wood. חכמים hold that the way we read it is what counts, and we read ונשל, meaning the iron itself slipped off its handle.
steps.whatsHappening: רב shows that both opinions in the משנה come from the same word. They differ on whether we learn from the spelling or from the reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without vowels, the letters can mean 'the iron knocked off' a chip from the tree, which is רבי's case of גלות. Read aloud, the word means 'the iron slipped off', which fits the head flying off the handle, the case where חכמים say גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: the written spelling is the main source for learning
the way the word is read aloud is the main source for learning
and it will make something slip off

steps.whatToRemember: רבי = יש אם למסורת (go by the spelling, ונישל). חכמים = יש אם למקרא (go by the reading, ונשל).
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties a practical question of גלות to a general rule about how we learn from the Torah's text.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב
phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi said that Rav said:
And both of them expounded one verse:
"And the iron slips from the wood."
Rabbi holds: the written form is authoritative,
phrases.notes: Literally 'there is a mother to the tradition': the way the letters are written is the root we learn from.

phrases.english: and it is written "and it made slip off";
phrases.notes: Same letters, different vowels: the iron knocked something else off, a chip from the tree.

phrases.english: and the Rabbis hold: the reading is authoritative,
and we read "and it slipped off."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם מִקְרָא אֶחָד דָּרְשׁוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different explanation of the root of the מחלוקת: both sides learn from the same word.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מחלוקת depends on יש אם למסורת (רבי) versus יש אם למקרא (חכמים) in the word ונשל.

steps.title: Does רבי really follow the written spelling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי really holds יש אם למסורת, as רב just said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי really hold that the written spelling is what counts?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's explanation of רבי's view. This line sets up the next move, where the גמרא will show why this is hard to accept.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב placed רבי on the side of יש אם למסורת. The question signals that elsewhere רבי seems to hold the opposite, so רב's explanation is now being tested.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי, יֵשׁ אֵם לַמָּסוֹרֶת סְבִירָא לֵיהּ?
phrases.english: And does Rabbi hold that the written form is authoritative?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי, יֵשׁ אֵם לַמָּסוֹרֶת סְבִירָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in the previous step that רבי holds יש אם למסורת.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that רבי holds יש אם למסורת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The question hints that רבי holds יש אם למקרא elsewhere, which would contradict רב's explanation. The proof comes on the next amud.
